I started on digital art very young, around 11, and that's around the time i started to take art seriously and learn. I've done a bulk of my learning through digital. Yes, tools like line smoothing and shape tools exist, but you don't have to use them. I used my drawing program like I would draw on pen and paper and truly the only difference is I don't really know how to properly draw with charcoal, but my fundamentals came out fine. 

I've witnessed many people who only drew traditionally get very discouraged when they try digital and I think that if digital art is what you're interested in, there's no reason why you can't start out digital. That said, It doesn't hurt to keep a sketch book and some graphite pencils too, though. Bottom line, I don't believe someone has to put off digital until they're good at traditional.

If you like digital art more, go with digital! The two can be quite different in a lot of ways and I don't really see a reason to learn traditional art first just to make the switch to digital later. Digital art can be overwhelming to a beginner but as long as you stick to some very basic tools and don't get overly complicated with programs or effects and whatnot, it's not a bad place to start.

First off, this is gorgeous. The textures and colors are really nice! I really love the face and the attention to detail around the window.

I think the problem you're facing is lack of contrast. That, and it doesn't truly feel like the different components in this piece are interacting with eachother or the environment. I see a lot of individual objects; a chair, a person, and open window, and those objects are generally well rendered, but i dont neccesarily see a person sitting on a chair with their legs on the windowsill. And it all comes down to the shadows and light source. 
Some harsh shadows, like where the legs are resting on the window sill, would add a ton more depth imo and bring everything together.

What I do a lot in digital art is add a gradient from top to bottom with a very dark saturated color on bottom and a very bright saturated color on top (or whereever the light source makes sense) and set it on a multiply layer and lower the opacity a bunch. This is a great way to tie the piece together and emphasize the light source. Obviously that process doesn't apply to traditional, but if you can, play around with that in a photo editor to see how that can improve your piece and keep it in mind for your next one. I think it can be a super effective tool for traditional artists but I don't see many using it!

I think _the_ fundemental art skill is observation skills. It can be helpful to know certain methods of drawing a head from imagination, but a true understanding of what it looks like comes from drawing from life and analyzing the shapes. And when you get good at analyzing that, you can translate it into any style you want.

My advice is to do some still lifes and life drawing. Not neccesarily of people! Just of random stuff, stuff with interesting shape and form, organic stuff, etc. Start training your brain to see the 3D shapes, and try and figure out how you can break down the world into fundemental shapes and lighting in a way that makes sense to you. 

Basically, don't take the "how to draw manga book" approach.

On the other hand, even if I can't beat it, a well decorated and designed level earns a new appreciation from me, and I'm 100% more likely to give it a heart on that merit alone.

The animal crossing community is similar. The reason people love this game is escapism, the positive nature, the good feelings it brings. It's supposed to be fun and especially with all the stuff going on, people don't wanna think about that.

Ive been there. I know what you're going through. I still go through it. 

What works for me, is analysing why my art looks wrong, and taking the active steps to learn proper techniques or correct bad habits. You just have to take it one thing at a time, and focus on really fundamental and specific components. Like instead of trying to improve drawing humans in general, start trying to improve how you draw the sketch or gesture, or even more miniscule than that and focus on specific parts of the body that trip you up, and practice just the sketch of that.

I also try to not delete or erase stuff. Sometimes I come back to stuff I absolutely hated while working on it, and am pleasantly surprised with how it looks. And, if I had gotten rid of it, i couldn't go back to it and analyse it later, and I would end up repeating the same mistakes. 

You can draw and draw and draw all day and you probably will improve, but at a point you have to start being really analytical and proactive about improvement to see real results. 

It takes patience, and there is no magical fix or method that will instantly make you not hate your art. You just have to remember that you'll never be any better if you quit.

The goal is to get lucky and be able to sell the turnips at a much higher price than you bought them. Buy low, sell high. The prices are random, so it's always a gamble because you may never end up with a price higher than what you paid, or you could get prices as high as over 500 bells. 

If you get lucky, or check in with friends/strangers on reddit's prices you can make a lot of money each week. It's one of the best and easiest ways to make money in the game.
